reading.rtitle: The Sentence With Nobody In It
paras: Adriana Vilas spent four years as chief financial officer of a software company that was bought twice, and she says the most useful thing she ever did there took one weekend. She rewrote the board pack. “Forty pages went to eleven,” she says. “Everybody noticed that. What nobody noticed was the grammar. In the old pack, almost every sentence had a person in it. In the new one, almost none did.”

Take one line. The old version read: my team missed the forecast because two large deals slipped. The new version read: the forecast was missed by nine percent; two deals moved into the next quarter. The facts are identical. But the first sentence asks the board to decide whether somebody should be blamed, and the second asks them to decide what to do next. “Boards are very good at the second question,” she says, “and almost useless at the first one.”

Where she put the people back was the part most finance teams leave anonymous. The accounts were audited by Vieira and Marsh in March tells a reader something. The accounts were audited tells them nothing, and a buyer asks the question anyway, two minutes later, in a worse tone. Her rule is short: if naming the actor changes the weight of the sentence, name the actor. She left churn and margin completely impersonal — churn is measured on client count, not on revenue — because there the definition is what matters and the person who chose it is not.

The rewrite also ended a habit she calls the most expensive one in corporate reporting: quoting the best month as if it were the shape of the whole year. “One quarter was an outlier and the entire company built a story on it. So we set a baseline — the trailing twelve months — and now every number in the pack is shown against that baseline and against an outside benchmark. It did not make anybody happier. It ended the arguments about whether a number was good, which is different and much more valuable.”

She is careful about the limits of the tool. “This grammar can be used to hide, and everybody in a board room knows that. If a sentence says a mistake was made, the room hears that somebody is not saying who, and you have just spent credibility to save one word. So there is one rule attached. Take the person out when the person is not the point. Never take the person out when the person is the point, and especially not when the person is you.” The pack she built is still in use. About a third of it is one page of recurring revenue, because that was the only page the second buyer read twice.

listenings.text: I read about two hundred board packs a year, and I can tell you what I do in the first ninety seconds. I look for the sentences that still have a person in them. Not because I want to know who did it, but because those are the sentences somebody fought over. Everything that was uncontroversial has already been flattened into the impersonal form: the accounts were audited, churn is measured this way, the numbers are shown against the benchmark. Nobody argues about those, so nobody is standing behind them. Then, in the middle of all that, you find one line that says my team delivered this, or the commercial director committed to that, and there is your fault line. That is where the disagreement lives. It is the only reliable way I know to find the real risk in a document that has been written by eight people who all wanted it to look calm.

Founders send us numbers and they think the number is the message. It is not. The definition is the message. If you tell me churn is eight percent, I have learned almost nothing, because I do not yet know what was counted. Eight percent of clients, or eight percent of revenue? Measured monthly and multiplied, or measured over the full year? Does a client who reduced their contract by half count as churn, or as nothing at all? Three companies can report the same eight percent and mean three different businesses. So write the definition into the sentence, every time, in the impersonal form: churn is measured on client count, not on revenue, over trailing twelve months. It takes eleven words. And when the numbers have been audited, say who audited them, because the name is doing work that the sentence cannot do without it.

extra_audio.text: Every figure on this page is shown against a trailing twelve-month baseline. Recurring revenue is now sixty-one percent of the total. Churn is measured on client count, and it sits below the market benchmark. One quarter was an outlier, so it was excluded from the baseline. The forecast was missed by nine percent, and the call behind it was mine. The accounts were audited by Vieira and Marsh in March, and the report is attached.
